items.title: I Watched GTA 6's In-Game TV Shows For Hours, They're Absolutely Wild
items.summary:
Of all the things I expected of Grand Theft Auto 6, sitting there watching in-game TV for like…two hours was not on my list. Freshly pre-loaded and ready to go on my Xbox Series X right at 3am on the west coast, claiming to be in New Zealand, booting it up for the first time had me rubbing my hands like Birdman – I was ready to get in the thick of it in GTA 6. What could this new Vice City's criminal underworld make me do? Not much. Will I have to survive shootouts early on, and will I need to contend with the new wanted system in a car chase? Not really. Mostly because as soon as I got to Jason's home in the opening hour, I sat my ass down on his living room couch, flipped on Weazel News and couldn't believe what I was seeing.

In GTA 6, you can sit on the couch and flip through three TV channels of original in-universe programming – full on TV shows made for the game, existing within the fiction of its world. You have Weazel News, the nutty right-wing parody that broadcasts news segments and TV series with the production value of something we'd see in our real world. Then there's the Telemundo spoof called Megamundo that shows Spanish-language soap operas / telenovelas, but with the absurdity cranked up several notches. Lastly, there's the Visit Leonida channel that's dedicated to advertising tourist attractions and businesses across this fictional rendition of Florida, satirizing modern economics and business.

"I'm always happy to keep playing him," Stan said, while appearing recently on the Next Best Picture podcast. "I don't know if the decision's up to me, ultimately. 

"I'm ready to take the character in all kinds of different ways," he continued, "but I can't make that decision, it's the powers that be. To be fair to Stan, after appearances in nine films and his own Disney+ spinoff, it's hard to know exactly where the character can continue to evolve. items.title: Why is GTA 6 Getting Review Bombed?
items.summary:
GTA 6 tied with the original version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-scored game in history based on Metacritic ratings, sitting pretty at a 99 critic score. Rarely do we see something earn this kind of unanimous praise, but our reviewer Luke Reilly would agree , giving GTA 6 a coveted score of 10 on our scale and calling it “the single most impressive video game I have ever played." However, you may have heard about the wide discrepancy between the critic's metascore and the user score — as of publishing this, GTA 6 has a 5.7/10 average from well over 100,000 user reviews. Why is that?

User scores on Metacritic are under far, far (and I mean far ) less scrutiny, allowing everyone and anyone to post their own review and score regardless of how much of the game they've actually played. This isn't anything new, and it’s been around on other sites that aggregate scores from the audience (like Rotten Tomatoes or an older version of GameSpot I used to use as a kid). As a result, you're likely to see more outliers or trolling, but mostly users who shoot from the hip to let their voice be heard. That leaves things susceptible to review bombing – typically, a wave of reactionary people who have motives beyond evaluating a game for what it is. 

There are reviews that appear to have legitimate concerns, mentioning that GTA 6 might not be for them or align with their tastes. Among those concerns are a slow start that emphasizes slice-of-life style activities before action starts to pick up, dissatisfaction with the interactive layers for simple tasks, the…

The Hisense UR8 RGB Mini-LED TV Gives OLED a Run for Its Money 

RGB Mini-LED is essentially the next generation evolution of Mini-LED technology. Traditional mini-LED TVs consist of an array of blue LED that are passed through RGB filters to produced the desired color. RGB Mini-LED TVs use red, green, and blue LEDs instead of just blue, which means the pixels no longer need filters to produce the desired color. The result is more accurate color reproduction, less blooming and, most importantly, a wider color gamut. In fact, the color gamut of RGB Mini-LED surpasses that of OLEDs, since current-generation OLEDs also use color filters combined with blue OLEDs. How does that translate in the real world? It means that you see richer, more accurate colors, smoother gradients and less banding than even OLEDs, especially in 4K HDR content.

1999's Thief Gold is widely considered the definitive incarnation of Thief: The Dark Project , adding three levels to the Looking Glass stealth sim while tidying up some bugs, but it has one grievous failing, in the eyes of many : the notorious Thieves Guild. In this all-new sixth mission, master catburglar Garrett must infiltrate the lair of a gang of pickpockets, after they filch a vase he had his eye on. The lair in question is actually very believable, as a hideout for criminals, in that it resists exploration even with a paper map. It consists of sunken, samey, obtusely arranged rooms that are made all the more headache-inducing by objectives that require a lot of backtracking.

In much the same way that I can admire a finely wrought pair of thumbscrews, I think the Thieves Guild is a clever creation, one that arguably shines when you use every ability or tactic in Garrett's possession rather than trying to ghost it. But it very easily becomes frustrating, to the point that many grizzled housebreakers advise new players to skip the level entirely. The Thieves Guild should be less frustrating in Nightdive's forthcoming Thief: The Dark Project Remastered , thanks to a more revealing spread of environmental textures and various other, furtive adjustments. As with many mods or remasters that speak of boosting the "immersion", I do worry that something valuable is being sacrificed in the process.

items.title: Queen's Domain review
items.summary: Where to start with Queen's Domain? It's tempting to begin with King's Field; after all, FromSoftware's seminal first-person action-RPG is an explicit inspiration for developer Freshly Baked Games. But 40 hours later, it feels like so much more. It's equally tempting to invoke another FromSoftware game: Dark Souls. Queen's Domain owes an obvious debt to that game's celebrated level design: the dazzling interconnectedness of its vertiginous world. But that's not quite right either. The deeper you delve, the more there's something of the spirit of The Legend of Zelda, a touch of Metroidvania too.
